abstract: Given a polygonal domain 𝒫 in the plane, the shortest path map with respect to a point s, denoted by SPM(s), is the decomposition of 𝒫 into cells such that shortest paths from s to all points t in the same cell have the same vertex sequence. The shortest path map equivalence decomposition of 𝒫 is the decomposition of 𝒫 into cells so that SPM(s) is topologically equivalent for all points s in the same cell. In this paper, we prove new upper bounds on the combinatorial complexities of the SPM-equivalence decompositions under various settings, depending on whether s and/or t are restricted to be the boundary of 𝒫. We also propose new algorithms to compute these decompositions. Further, our results lead to new solutions to several other problems, including answering two-point shortest path queries in 𝒫, and computing geodesic diameter and center of 𝒫.

      Abstract
Given a polygonal domain P in the plane, the shortest path map with respect to a point s, denoted
by SPM (s), is the decomposition of P into cells such that shortest paths from s to all points t in
the same cell have the same vertex sequence. The shortest path map equivalence decomposition of
P is the decomposition of P into cells so that SPM (s) is topologically equivalent for all points s
in the same cell. In this paper, we prove new upper bounds on the combinatorial complexities of
the SPM -equivalence decompositions under various settings, depending on whether s and/or t are
restricted to be the boundary of P. We also propose new algorithms to compute these decompositions.
Further, our results lead to new solutions to several other problems, including answering two-point
shortest path queries in P, and computing geodesic diameter and center of P.

 1      Introduction
Let P be a polygonal domain of h holes with a total of n vertices in the plane, i.e., P is a
closed and multiply-connected region bounded by n segments that form h + 1 cycles (holes
and the region outside P are also called obstacles). The shortest path map (or SPM for
short) with respect to a point s ∈ P, denoted by SPM (s), is the decomposition of P into
cells such that shortest paths from s to all points t in the same cell are combinatorially the
same (i.e., they have the same vertex sequence) [10, 23]; see Fig. 1. The SPM-equivalence
decomposition of P, denoted by Ψ, is the decomposition of P into cells so that SPM (s) is
topologically equivalent for all points s in the same cell. Chiang and Mitchell [10] first studied
the SPM-equivalence decomposition and used it to answer two-point shortest path queries in
P. They proved that the combinatorial complexity of Ψ is bounded by O(n10 ) and proposed
an O(n10 log n) time algorithm to compute it.
    We consider several variants of the SPM-equivalence decompositions, depending on
whether s and/or t are required to be on the boundary of P . Specifically, let B denote
the boundary of P. We define the boundary-restricted shortest path map for a point s,
denoted by SPMB (s), as the decomposition of B into segments such that shortest paths
from s to all points t in the same segment are combinatorially the same. We define the
boundary-restricted SPM-equivalence decomposition with respect to P (resp., B), denoted
by ΨB (P) (resp., ΨB (B)), as the decomposition of B into segments so that SPM (s) (resp.,
SPMB (s)) are topologically equivalent for all points s in the same segment. Similarly, we
let ΨP (B) denote the decomposition of P into cells so that SPMB (s) is topologically the
same for all points s in the same cell. If we follow the same convention for notation, then
ΨP (P) is Ψ (we will use the two notations interchangeably). Another way to view these

1.1     An overview of our approach
To bound |ΨB (B)|, we reduce the problem to analyzing the combinatorial complexities of lower
envelopes of certain functions. For each vertex u of P, we define a set of functions fu (s, t) as
follows. Let Vis(u) denote the visibility polygon of u in P. For each edge et ∈ SPMB (u), et
lies in a single cell of SPM (u), and let vt be the root of the cell. For each edge es of Vis(u) ∩ B,
define a function fu (s, t) = |su| + d(u, vt ) + |vt t|, for s ∈ es and t ∈ et , where d(u, vt ) is the
geodesic distance between u and vt . Since both Vis(u) ∩ B and SPMB (u) have O(n) edges,
the above defines O(n2 ) bivariate functions (of constant degree) for u, each of which defines a
constant-sized two-dimensional surface patch in R3 . As P has O(n) vertices, we have O(n3 )
functions in total; let F denote the set of all of these functions. Our first observation is that
a vertex of ΨB (B) corresponds to a vertex of the lower envelope L(F ) of (the surface patches
defined by) the functions of F . Hence, it suffices to analyze the complexity of L(F ).
     To find a bound for |L(F )|, one could apply the result of Sharir [34], who proved an
O(nd+ϵ ) upper bound for the size of the lower envelope of a collection of n constant-sized
(partially defined) d-variate algebraic functions of constant degree, for any d ≥ 2 (the d = 2
case was first proved in [18]; see also [35, Chapter 7]). Since |F | = O(n3 ) and d = 2 in
our problem, applying the above result directly could obtain an upper bound O(n6+ϵ ) for
|L(F )|. We instead take a closer look at the problem. Our main idea is that we find a way
to decompose the lower envelope L(F ) into O(n2 ) regions so that for each region it suffices
to consider O(n) functions of F . Consequently, by applying the algorithm of [18, 34, 35] for
each region, we can prove an upper bound of O(n4+ϵ ) for |L(F )| and thus for |ΨB (B)|, and
also compute the vertices of L(F ) and thus compute ΨB (B) in O(n4+ϵ ) time.
     For ΨB (P), a simple brute-force approach can provide a good upper bound for its size
(similar techniques were used before for related problems [3, 10, 38]). To compute ΨB (P),
since it is a decomposition of B, which is one-dimensional, we use a sweeping point algorithm,
i.e., moving a point s on B and find those event points when SPM (s) changes combinatorially.
     For ΨP (P), unfortunately, our approach does not yield a better result than the O(n10 )
bound from [10]. One reason is that the decomposition is on P, which is two-dimensional,
and a vertex of it might not correspond to a vertex of the lower envelope of the corresponding

     For any compact region R in the plane, let ∂R denote its boundary. Recall that B is the
boundary of P. For differentiation, we often refer to the vertices of P as obstacle vertices
and the edges of P as obstacle edges.
     For any point p in P, let Vis(p) denote the visibility polygon of p, i.e., Vis(p) consists of all
points q ∈ P such that pq ⊆ P. The size of Vis(p) is O(n) [19]. Define VisB (p) = Vis(p) ∩ B,
i.e., the portions of B that are visible to p, which consists of O(n) segments on B.

Shortest path maps. The shortest path map SPM (s) of a point s ∈ P is a decomposition
of P into cells such that all points t in the cell σ have the same anchor in any shortest s-t
path [23, 29]; the anchor is called the root of σ. Each edge of SPM (s) is an obstacle edge
fragment, an extension segment (i.e., extended from an obstacle vertex u in the direction
away from v, where v is the anchor of u in a shortest s-u path), or a bisector curve which is
the locus of points p with d(s, u) + |pu| = d(s, v) + |pv| for two obstacle vertices u and v. See
Fig. 1. Although an extension segment can be viewed as a degenerated bisector curve, we use
bisector curve to refer to the general case only. As such, any point on a bisector curve has
two topologically different paths from s. As in [13], we call the intersection of two bisector
curves a triple point, which has at least three topologically different shortest paths from s.
    It is known that SPM (s) is of size O(n) [23, 30] and can be computed in O(n log n)
time [23] or in O(n + h log h) time after P is triangulated [39] (note that triangulating P can
be done in O(n + h log h) time by a recent algorithm of Chan [7]).
    Recall that SPMB (s) refers to the portion of SPM (s) restricted to B, the boundary of P.
Hence, SPMB (s) consists of a set of segments each of which belongs to a cell of SPM (s).

Shortest path trees (SPT) and SPT-equivalence decompositions. For a point s ∈ P, the
shortest path tree, denoted by SPT (s), is a spanning tree of s and the vertices of P such that
the path in the tree from s to any vertex is a shortest path in P.
    The SPT-equivalence decomposition of P, denoted by Ψspt , is the subdivision of P into
cells such that SPT (s) is combinatorially the same for all points s in the same cell. The
decomposition Ψspt can be obtained by overlaying SPM (u) for all obstacle vertices u of
